interactions.label: Why are the forensic tasks of establishing corpus delicti and identifying an unk

params.question: Why are the forensic tasks of establishing corpus delicti and identifying an unknown person considered legally distinct?

answers.text: Because identification must always be completed before corpus delicti can be established

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: There is no mandatory sequence — corpus delicti and identification are parallel but independent tasks. A crime can be proved without knowing the victim, and a victim can be identified without proving a crime.

answers.text: Because corpus delicti requires proof that a crime occurred, while identification requires systematic assessment of biological characteristics — each uses different evidence and methods

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Corpus delicti is a legal doctrine proving that a crime took place; identification is a biological exercise assessing race, sex, complexion, stature, and individualising features. Each demands different evidence, methods, and standards of proof.

answers.text: Because Indian law requires separate medicolegal reports for each task

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both tasks can be addressed within the same medicolegal examination and report. They are logically distinct, not procedurally separated into different reports.

answers.text: Because corpus delicti applies only to homicides, while identification applies to all deaths

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Corpus delicti applies to any crime — theft, assault, homicide — not only to homicide. Similarly, identification is needed for any unknown person, whether living or dead.

overallFeedback.feedback: Corpus delicti is the proof that a crime occurred — it is a legal doctrine, not a body. Identification is a separate biological exercise. Each requires different evidence and methods; confusing the two can derail both the investigation and the prosecution.
Exactly right. Recognising that 'Was this a crime?' and 'Who is this person?' require fundamentally different evidence is the first step in any forensic examination of an unknown body.

params.question: A magistrate asks you to determine whether an accused person is above or below 25 years of age. Which single X-ray site would be most informative for this determination?

answers.text: Wrist — lower end of radius and ulna

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wrist epiphyses fuse by approximately 17–19 years. They are useful for assessing whether a person is above 16–18 years but cannot distinguish the 25-year threshold.
The olecranon fuses by approximately 16–17 years, making it informative for younger age thresholds but far too early to address the 25-year question.
The lower femoral epiphysis fuses by approximately 20 years. While useful for mid-range age estimation, it provides no information about whether someone has crossed 25 years.

The medial epiphysis of the clavicle is the last epiphysis to fuse in the human body, completing fusion by approximately 25 years. Complete fusion at this site is the most reliable skeletal indicator that a person is above 25 years of age.

overallFeedback.feedback: The medial epiphysis of the clavicle is the last epiphysis to fuse in the body. For the 25-year threshold, it is the only site whose fusion timeline spans that critical age — all other common sites fuse well before 25.

Correct. The medial clavicular epiphysis appears at 16–18 years and fuses completely by about 25 years — making it the single most valuable site for medicolegal age estimation in the young-adult range.

interactions.label: After examining skeletal remains for a police requisition that asks only for sex

params.question: After examining skeletal remains for a police requisition that asks only for sex and stature estimation, your examination also reveals distinctive dental features. How should these dental findings be documented in your report?

answers.text: Include them in the same section as the requested findings without any distinction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mixing volunteered and requested findings without distinction can be challenged in court. The report must clearly attribute which observations were solicited and which were offered independently.

answers.text: Document them separately and clearly mark them as volunteered observations beyond the scope of the requisition

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Findings beyond the requisition's scope must be recorded separately and explicitly noted as volunteered. This preserves potentially valuable forensic evidence while maintaining transparency about what was asked for and what was independently observed.

answers.text: Omit them entirely since they were not part of the requisition

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Withholding relevant forensic observations would be professionally negligent. The doctor should record all findings but must distinguish solicited observations from volunteered ones.

answers.text: Communicate them verbally to the investigating officer but exclude them from the written report

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: All forensic findings must be part of the written record. Verbal-only communication has no evidential value in court and leaves no auditable trail.

overallFeedback.feedback: The forensic doctor must not go beyond the questions asked without clearly noting that additional observations are volunteered. This distinction — solicited versus volunteered — is fundamental to a legally defensible medicolegal report.
Well done. Clearly separating volunteered observations from requisitioned findings is essential for both scientific integrity and legal defensibility of the forensic report.
